pieces.title: Accredited investor: the SEC's three tests for an individual

content.text: Raising from friends and family? Check one thing first: is each of them an accredited investor? A short thread on the SEC's tests for an individual, with an example.
thread: Test 1, income: an individual is an accredited investor with income over $200,000, or over $300,000 with a spouse or spousal equivalent, in each of the last two years, and reasonably expects the same this year.
Test 2, net worth: an individual also qualifies with a net worth over $1 million, alone or with a spouse or spousal equivalent, not counting their primary residence.
Test 3, a license: an individual also qualifies by holding a Series 7, 65 or 82 license in good standing.

Worked example: a friend whose net worth is over $1 million only when their home is counted does not pass the net worth test, since the primary residence is not counted. They may still qualify on income or a license.

pieces.title: Rule 506(c): advertise your raise, then verify

content.text: Want to talk about your raise in public? Rule 506(c) is the route for that. A short thread on what it allows and what it asks, with an example.
thread: The rule: under Rule 506(c), a company can advertise its raise broadly, but every purchaser must be accredited and the company must take reasonable steps to verify it, such as reviewing tax returns or bank statements.

The other route: under Rule 506(b), a company cannot use general solicitation or advertising, and can sell to any number of accredited investors plus up to 35 other purchasers who are financially sophisticated, alone or with a representative.
Worked example: a round advertised broadly under Rule 506(c) cannot take money from a purchaser who is not accredited, even one who is financially sophisticated.

pieces.title: Music reel: Your 2027 filing calendar: five dates from February to June

captions.instagram:
Five dates for your US company, February to June 2027.

February 1: Forms 1099-NEC for 2026 payments go to each payee and to the IRS by Monday, February 1, 2027, since January 31, 2027 is a Sunday.

March 1 and March 31: Delaware corporations file their annual report and pay franchise tax by March 1 each year; in 2027 that is a Monday. Form 1099-MISC for 2026 is due to the IRS by Monday, March 1, 2027 on paper, or by Wednesday, March 31, 2027 when filed electronically.

April 15: A calendar year C corporation's Form 1120 for 2026 is due by Thursday, April 15, 2027; Form 7004, filed by that date, gives an automatic six month extension of time to file, to Friday, October 15, 2027.

June 1: A Delaware LLC pays an annual tax of $400, due by June 1 for the year before.
